plan.hypothesis: A plain masked elementwise kernel with BLOCK=4096 will pass all 30 correctness cases and give a first measured speedup profile that shows which workloads are host-launch bound versus bandwidth bound

expected_effect.mechanism: Establish a correct, compilable baseline and a per-workload speedup map

profile.summary: mixed: Small/medium timing workloads are host-launch bound: device kernel is 2.69 us against 62.75 us eval latency, Large 4096x4096 cases are vector-instruction bound, not bandwidth bound; fp16 and fp32 take near-identical time at 2x byte difference, Masked load/store path is executed for every program even where the grid exactly divides N; scalar pipe is 15-16% of large-case device time

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline established (30/30 PASSED, geo_mean 0.2305, min 0.170). Two distinct losses: (1) nine small timing workloads sit on a flat 62.8-70.0 us floor while the msprof device kernel lasts only 2.694 us, so ~60 us per call is host/launch overhead (reference torch.round is 14.2-15.8 us total); (2) the three 4096x4096 workloads are device bound at 176-186 us and are vector-instruction bound, not memory bound: fp16 fp16 4096^2 moves 67.1 MB in 176.13 us (381 GB/s) while fp32 4096^2 moves 134.2 MB in 185.66 us (723 GB/s), i.e. doubling bytes costs only +5.4% time, so the ~12-14 fp32 vector ops per element dominate (vec ratio 0.58-0.68, mte2 only 0.12-0.20, aic 0).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected a first measured map, observed it. All 12 timing workloads lose: small ones 0.21-0.24x with 4.3% of the call in the device kernel (host overhead dominance, profile-confirmed), large ones 0.18-0.44x with time scaling with element count rather than bytes (instruction dominance). Correctness is exact where expected (abs_err 0 for 16 of 18 correctness cases, <=2.4e-7 for the two decimals!=0 cases, matched_ratio 1.0 everywhere).
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the host launch path first since it controls 9 of 12 timing workloads: replace the per-call Kernel[grid](...) dispatch with a cached compiled-artifact low-level launch keyed on (dtype, DECIMALS, BLOCK, layout kind) that passes current pointers, current N, current SCALE/INV_SCALE and the current stream each call, keeping the kernel body, strided path and NaN/Inf handling unchanged behind a fallback branch. Verify the exact launcher signature on the target with one bounded debug job before submitting.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Device-side msprof on a 1024-element case (2.694 us kernel inside a 62.75 us call) was the only way to separate host overhead from kernel cost; the flat latency floor across a 1024x element range was the leading indicator but the 4.3% device share made it conclusive.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: From 'write a correct simple kernel' to a two-front plan ordered by measured share: host launch overhead for the 9 small workloads, then fp32-emulation vector op count for the 3 large ones.

plan.code_changes: Added _stream_getter / _pick_block / _direct_launcher / _guarded helpers and per-key plans: the first call per (dtype, numel, decimals, layout) calls jitfn.warmup once and caches a closure that issues launcher.launch(gridX,1,1,current_raw_stream,function,packed_metadata,None,None,None, x_ptr, out_ptr, N, SCALE, INV_SCALE, DECIMALS, BLOCK). Pointers, N, scalars and the stream handle are re-passed every call; unaligned pointers or any launcher exception drop back to the bound JIT call. Kernel bodies, strided indexing and NaN/Inf handling are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: Round-1 msprof showed timing-0 spends 2.694 us in the device kernel inside a 62.75 us call while the reference torch.round finishes in 14.25 us, so ~60 us per call is host launch overhead; driving the compiled Ascend launcher directly (validated pattern from the batch's xlogy runtime-scalar-v3 proposal) should bring the nine small workloads from ~63-70 us to well below 30 us while leaving device-bound large workloads within a few percent

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing the per-call JIT binder/cache-key/arg-packing work drops the ~60 us fixed cost that currently dominates the nine small workloads, whose device kernel is only 2.694 us

conclusion.root_cause: The nine small workloads were host-launch bound: ~60 us of per-call Triton JIT binding overhead around a 2.694 us device kernel. Driving the compiled Ascend launcher from a cached closure removed that, leaving ~14.5 us of per-call host cost. The three 4096x4096 workloads are untouched device-side and remain vector-instruction bound (~12 fp32 vector ops per element, vec ratio 0.58-0.68, time scaling with elements not bytes).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted geo_mean 0.45-0.55 from the launch change alone; observed 0.5866, slightly better. The nine small workloads landed at 16.5-17.4 us (0.799-0.882x) versus the 14.0-14.5 us reference, so the ~60 us overhead collapsed as expected and only ~3 us of per-call host cost above the reference remains. The three large workloads moved only within noise (timing-3 173.0 -> 174.4 us, timing-7 172.8 -> 178.8 us, timing-11 180.4 -> 182.5 us), exactly as predicted since their device kernels are unchanged; their reported speedups shifted (timing-7 0.170 -> 0.107, timing-11 0.437 -> 0.509) mostly because the reference timings themselves moved (timing-7 reference 29.4 -> 19.2 us, timing-11 78.9 -> 92.8 us), not because of the candidate. Correctness identical to round 1 (matched_ratio 1.0, max abs_err 2.4e-7).
conclusion.next_suggestion: With the host floor fixed, attack the three device-bound 4096x4096 workloads by cutting fp32 vector ops per element from ~12 to ~7 in _rnd_value: one integer magnitude mask, one integer compare against 0x4B000000 (which covers |v|>=2^23, Inf and NaN in a single test), the 2^23 add/sub pair, one sign-bit mask plus or, and one select; skip the SCALE multiply when DECIMALS==0. Worth 3 of 12 timing workloads at 0.11-0.51.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A flat latency floor across a 1024x element range plus a 4.3% device share was the correct read: the launch path, not the kernel, owned the small workloads. After the fix the same workloads sit at 17.2 us with a 2.7 us device kernel, i.e. ~14.5 us of host cost remains against the reference's ~12.5 us.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 established that nothing is HBM bound (small = launch bound, large = fp32-emulation instruction bound). Round 2 removed the launch-bound half, so the remaining work is entirely device-side vector instruction count plus a small residual host cost.

plan.strategy: Reduce per-call host cost with a single-entry memoised raw-launch fast path
plan.code_changes: run() now first tries a single-entry memo fast path (pointer/dtype/numel/contiguity/decimals checks) that calls the cached raw Triton launcher directly; the previous multi-step Python prelude (out-None check, shape/dtype/device validation, tuple-key plan lookup, alignment test) moved into _slow(), which is only entered on a memo miss. Kernel code is byte-identical to round 1.
plan.hypothesis: The nine small/medium workloads (1024 to 1048576 elements) are dominated by host overhead, not device time, so removing Python bookkeeping per call raises their speedup from ~0.86 toward parity without touching kernel behaviour.

expected_effect.mechanism: Nine of twelve timing workloads are launch-overhead bound; measured host decomposition showed a ~9.9us raw launcher floor plus ~5.4us of run() bookkeeping (meta6 1.77us, data_ptr 0.51us, plan lookup, dict key). Collapsing the prelude to ~6 cheap C-level checks removes roughly 3-4us per call.

conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: remove 3-4us of per-call host overhead so the nine launch-bound workloads approach parity. Observed: all nine moved from 0.84-0.88 to 1.18-1.23 (timing-0 0.879->1.232, -1 0.856->1.184, -2 0.863->1.200, -4 0.880->1.184, -5 0.843->1.184, -6 0.858->1.217, -8 0.857->1.182, -9 0.866->1.200, -10 0.844->1.201), with latency dropping from 17.3-18.5us to 12.6-13.3us while references stayed 15.5-16.1us. The three large workloads were untouched by design (timing-3 0.287, timing-7 0.172, timing-11 0.777 vs 0.693 in round 1, the latter only because the reference timing drifted from 92.4us to 106.1us while our latency was flat at 133-137us). Geo mean 0.6742 -> 0.8728, slightly better than the predicted ~0.82 because the fast path removed the full prelude rather than part of it.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the three 4096x4096 workloads by shrinking the rounding core: the FP32 magic-number sequence currently uses ~14 vector ops (11 plus two dtype conversions plus the redundant NaN/Inf select and a redundant AND before the sign OR) at ~7.1us per op over 16.7M elements. Replace it with the minimal exact 9-op form (conversion, abs, add, sub, cmp, select, and, or, conversion) which is bitwise-equivalent for ties, negative zero, NaN and Inf, and for FP32 dtype lands at 7 ops, below the measured 89us memory floor for that shape.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The host cost decomposition (raw launcher 9.9us, run() prelude 5.4us, torch_npu raw stream getter 0.26us vs Triton driver getter 4.77us) predicted the gain correctly; the Triton JIT dispatch path on this target costs ~50us and must be avoided on every call.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Host path is now near its floor; remaining loss is entirely in the three 4096x4096 workloads, which are vector-compute bound rather than memory bound.

plan.strategy: Minimal exact FP32 magic-number rounding core
plan.code_changes: _value() now: converts to fp32, applies decimals scaling only when DECIMALS!=0, computes magnitude, applies the 2^23 magic round with the large-magnitude clamp, and restores the sign by OR-ing the input sign bit into the (always non-negative) rounded value. Removed the explicit isnan/isinf select (NaN/Inf propagate through the magic unchanged) and the redundant AND-mask before the sign OR. Kernels and host fast path unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The three 4096x4096 workloads are bound by the number of FP32 vector ops in the rounding core, so removing the redundant NaN/Inf select and the sign mask lowers their latency by roughly 30% while staying bitwise-exact for ties, negative zero, NaN and Inf.

expected_effect.mechanism: Vector op count over 16.7M elements drops from ~14 fp32 ops to 9 for bf16/fp16 and to 7 for fp32; at the measured ~7.1us per fp32 vector op this removes roughly 30-35us from the 16-bit workloads and pushes the fp32 workload from 136us toward the 89us memory floor.

conclusion.root_cause: The rounding core was still issuing reducible FP32 vector work (NaN/Inf select, sign mask) and was compute-bound; on Ascend an FP32 vector op over 16.7M elements costs ~7us, so op count directly sets the large-shape latency.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: ~30% lower latency on the three 4096x4096 workloads by cutting the core from ~14 to 9/7 FP32 vector ops. Observed: timing-3 109.8->66.8us (0.287->0.471), timing-7 111.7->68.0us (0.172->0.320), timing-11 136.6->103.6us (0.777->0.915) - a 1.64x, 1.64x and 1.32x latency reduction, matching the op-count model (each removed FP32 vector op is worth ~7us over 16.7M elements). All 30 workloads stayed numerically exact, confirming the removed NaN/Inf select and sign mask were redundant. The nine launch-bound workloads were unchanged in absolute terms (12.6-13.3us -> 13.0-14.7us, within noise) but their reference latencies fell 13%, so their speedup ratios dropped from 1.18-1.23 to 0.94-1.04 and the aggregate geo mean moved 0.873->0.853 despite a genuinely 1.6x faster kernel on the shapes that dominate absolutely.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-apply the minimal core and add a native 16-bit path for bf16/fp16 that avoids the constructs that made the earlier native attempt numerically wrong (no 16-bit bitcast for sign restore and no tl.abs on 16-bit; use where-based magnitude and sign), since 16-bit vector ops cost about half an FP32 op and the two 16-bit shapes are still 3-5x above the 12.5us copy floor. Also push the FP32 shape from 103.6us toward its measured 89.3us memory floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Reference-side latency on launch-bound workloads moved 15.5->13.5us between rounds 2 and 3 and a retest verified the new value as stable, so cross-round geo_mean comparisons are confounded at the ~9% level on nine of twelve workloads; absolute candidate latency is the reliable signal for the large shapes.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Large shapes now scale with vector op count, not memory; the next lever is switching bf16/fp16 to native 16-bit arithmetic while keeping exactness for ties, negative zero, NaN and Inf.

method.note: Minimal exact FP32 magic-number rounding core

plan.strategy: Native 16-bit magic-number rounding core for bf16/fp16
plan.code_changes: Re-applied the minimal FP32 core (round 3) and added a native 16-bit path used whenever decimals==0 and dtype is bf16/fp16: neg = x<0, magnitude = where(neg,-x,x), rounded = (magnitude+M)-M with M=1024.0 (fp16) or 128.0 (bf16), clamp at M, result = where(neg,-rounded,rounded). No 16-bit bitcast and no tl.abs on 16-bit, so it cannot fail through the two constructs that broke the earlier native attempt. decimals!=0 keeps the exact FP32 scale/div_rn path.
plan.hypothesis: The bf16 and fp16 4096x4096 workloads are bound by FP32 vector throughput at ~7us per op; expressing the identical exact rounding in native 16-bit arithmetic nearly halves that cost, while remaining bit-exact for ties, negative zero, NaN, Inf and large magnitudes.

expected_effect.mechanism: 16-bit vector ops cost roughly half an FP32 op on the AIV unit; replacing 9 FP32-equivalent op slots (7 ops plus 2 conversions) with 9 native 16-bit slots cuts the two 16-bit large-shape latencies from ~68us toward ~40us.

conclusion.root_cause: The Ascend Triton backend promotes bf16/fp16 arithmetic to FP32, so a 16-bit magic constant cannot round and the native path adds promotion cost on top; native 16-bit vector throughput is not available through this compiler.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: native 16-bit arithmetic roughly halves the two 16-bit large-shape latencies. Observed the opposite and a correctness break: timing-3 66.8->77.3us, timing-7 68.0->126.8us (1.16x and 1.86x slower than the FP32 core), with correctness-6, correctness-8 and correctness-10 failing at matched_ratio 0.0/0.048/0.048. The failure signature (abs_err 0.36-0.5, ~5% matched, i.e. values that were already integral) is the identity, showing the add/sub pair was executed in FP32 with a 1024/128 magic that cannot round there. The FP32 core from round 3 remains the best formulation and timing-11 stayed at 103.6us across both rounds, confirming the fp32 path is unchanged.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the FP32 core but exploit a proven exactness property instead of the clamp: every fp16/bf16 value is a multiple of the FP32 ulp at its magnitude, so the 2^23 magic is already exact for the whole 16-bit input domain and the magnitude clamp can be dropped for those dtypes. Combine that with a signed magic constant m = +-2^23 chosen by sign, which removes both tl.abs and the sign bit-restore, giving 6 op slots (input conversion, compare, select, add, sub, output conversion) instead of 9 for bf16/fp16, and keep the clamped 7-op FP32 path only for the fp32 dtype where the shape is memory-bound anyway.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this backend 16-bit arithmetic is promoted to FP32 before execution: a 1024.0/128.0 magic therefore never rounds, and the extra promotion/demotion slots made the native kernel slower than the FP32 core. Any rounding scheme must use the 2^23 FP32 magic.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Native 16-bit arithmetic is closed off; remaining gains must come from reducing FP32 op slots in the 16-bit path, which is exactly 2 conversions plus the magic work.

method.note: Native 16-bit magic-number rounding core for bf16/fp16

plan.strategy: Native 16-bit magic-number rounding core for bf16/fp16
plan.code_changes: Re-applied the minimal FP32 core (round 3) and added a native 16-bit path used whenever decimals==0 and dtype is bf16/fp16: neg = x<0, magnitude = where(neg,-x,x), rounded = (magnitude+M)-M with M=1024.0 (fp16) or 128.0 (bf16), clamp at M, result = where(neg,-rounded,rounded). No 16-bit bitcast and no tl.abs on 16-bit, so it cannot fail through the two constructs that broke the earlier native attempt. decimals!=0 keeps the exact FP32 scale/div_rn path.
plan.hypothesis: The bf16 and fp16 4096x4096 workloads are bound by FP32 vector throughput at ~7us per op; expressing the identical exact rounding in native 16-bit arithmetic nearly halves that cost, while remaining bit-exact for ties, negative zero, NaN, Inf and large magnitudes.

expected_effect.mechanism: 16-bit vector ops cost roughly half an FP32 op on the AIV unit; replacing 9 FP32-equivalent op slots (7 ops plus 2 conversions) with 9 native 16-bit slots cuts the two 16-bit large-shape latencies from ~68us toward ~40us.

conclusion.root_cause: The Ascend Triton backend promotes bf16/fp16 arithmetic to FP32, so a 16-bit magic constant cannot round and the native path adds promotion cost on top; native 16-bit vector throughput is not available through this compiler.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: native 16-bit arithmetic roughly halves the two 16-bit large-shape latencies. Observed the opposite and a correctness break: timing-3 66.8->77.3us, timing-7 68.0->126.8us (1.16x and 1.86x slower than the FP32 core), with correctness-6, correctness-8 and correctness-10 failing at matched_ratio 0.0/0.048/0.048. The failure signature (abs_err 0.36-0.5, ~5% matched, i.e. values that were already integral) is the identity, showing the add/sub pair was executed in FP32 with a 1024/128 magic that cannot round there. The FP32 core from round 3 remains the best formulation and timing-11 stayed at 103.6us across both rounds, confirming the fp32 path is unchanged.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the FP32 core but exploit a proven exactness property instead of the clamp: every fp16/bf16 value is a multiple of the FP32 ulp at its magnitude, so the 2^23 magic is already exact for the whole 16-bit input domain and the magnitude clamp can be dropped for those dtypes. Combine that with a signed magic constant m = +-2^23 chosen by sign, which removes both tl.abs and the sign bit-restore, giving 6 op slots (input conversion, compare, select, add, sub, output conversion) instead of 9 for bf16/fp16, and keep the clamped 7-op FP32 path only for the fp32 dtype where the shape is memory-bound anyway.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this backend 16-bit arithmetic is promoted to FP32 before execution: a 1024.0/128.0 magic therefore never rounds, and the extra promotion/demotion slots made the native kernel slower than the FP32 core. Any rounding scheme must use the 2^23 FP32 magic.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Native 16-bit arithmetic is closed off; remaining gains must come from reducing FP32 op slots in the 16-bit path, which is exactly 2 conversions plus the magic work.

plan.code_changes: Re-applied the minimal FP32 core (round 3) and added a native 16-bit path used whenever decimals==0 and dtype is bf16/fp16: neg = x<0, magnitude = where(neg,-x,x), rounded = (magnitude+M)-M with M=1024.0 (fp16) or 128.0 (bf16), clamp at M, result = where(neg,-rounded,rounded). No 16-bit bitcast and no tl.abs on 16-bit, so it cannot fail through the two constructs that broke the earlier native attempt. decimals!=0 keeps the exact FP32 scale/div_rn path.
plan.hypothesis: The bf16 and fp16 4096x4096 workloads are bound by FP32 vector throughput at ~7us per op; expressing the identical exact rounding in native 16-bit arithmetic nearly halves that cost, while remaining bit-exact for ties, negative zero, NaN, Inf and large magnitudes.

expected_effect.mechanism: 16-bit vector ops cost roughly half an FP32 op on the AIV unit; replacing 9 FP32-equivalent op slots (7 ops plus 2 conversions) with 9 native 16-bit slots cuts the two 16-bit large-shape latencies from ~68us toward ~40us.

conclusion.root_cause: The Ascend Triton backend promotes bf16/fp16 arithmetic to FP32, so a 16-bit magic constant cannot round and the native path adds promotion cost on top; native 16-bit vector throughput is not available through this compiler.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Frozen expectation: native 16-bit arithmetic roughly halves the two 16-bit large-shape latencies. Observed the opposite and a correctness break: timing-3 66.8->77.3us, timing-7 68.0->126.8us (1.16x and 1.86x slower than the FP32 core), with correctness-6, correctness-8 and correctness-10 failing at matched_ratio 0.0/0.048/0.048. The failure signature (abs_err 0.36-0.5, ~5% matched, i.e. values that were already integral) is the identity, showing the add/sub pair was executed in FP32 with a 1024/128 magic that cannot round there. The FP32 core from round 3 remains the best formulation and timing-11 stayed at 103.6us across both rounds, confirming the fp32 path is unchanged.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Keep the FP32 core but exploit a proven exactness property instead of the clamp: every fp16/bf16 value is a multiple of the FP32 ulp at its magnitude, so the 2^23 magic is already exact for the whole 16-bit input domain and the magnitude clamp can be dropped for those dtypes. Combine that with a signed magic constant m = +-2^23 chosen by sign, which removes both tl.abs and the sign bit-restore, giving 6 op slots (input conversion, compare, select, add, sub, output conversion) instead of 9 for bf16/fp16, and keep the clamped 7-op FP32 path only for the fp32 dtype where the shape is memory-bound anyway.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this backend 16-bit arithmetic is promoted to FP32 before execution: a 1024.0/128.0 magic therefore never rounds, and the extra promotion/demotion slots made the native kernel slower than the FP32 core. Any rounding scheme must use the 2^23 FP32 magic.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Native 16-bit arithmetic is closed off; remaining gains must come from reducing FP32 op slots in the 16-bit path, which is exactly 2 conversions plus the magic work.
